notes.meaning: David was about seventy years old, worn out by years of battle, hard work, and deep grief. Even with many blankets over him, his body could no longer keep warm. His growing weakness showed that his long reign was coming to an end.

David's royal servants, acting as his doctors, recommended an ancient medical remedy to restore his failing strength. They suggested bringing a healthy young woman to serve the king and sleep close to him so her body heat would warm him. In the ancient world, people saw this as a practical way to revive an elderly, failing body.

The servants searched throughout the land of Israel to find a suitable, beautiful young woman for the king. They found Abishag from the town of Shunem, in the territory of Issachar, and brought her to Jerusalem. Her beauty ensured that she would be pleasing and acceptable in the royal court.

Abishag was extraordinarily beautiful, and she looked after King David's personal needs. David had no sexual relations with her, which showed how frail his health was and made it clear that she served only as his nurse. Her position in the royal household later became a major issue in the struggle for the throne.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church father Jerome rejected a literal reading, interpreting Abishag allegorically as divine wisdom that remains warm even as the physical body grows old.

notes.meaning: David's son Adonijah took advantage of his father's failing health to make a bid for the throne. Since his older brothers had died, he assumed he was next in line and openly declared himself king. Just like his brother Absalom before him, he gathered chariots, horses, and fifty runners to make a grand royal show.

David had spoiled Adonijah his entire life, never questioning his actions or correcting his bad behavior. Adonijah was also very handsome and was born next after Absalom, which made him popular and self-confident. A lack of loving discipline at home helped fuel his arrogant grab for power.

Adonijah sought the support of two powerful leaders: Joab, the commander of the army, and Abiathar, one of the leading priests. Joab gave him military backing, while Abiathar gave his claim religious authority. Both men had grown distant from David and hoped to secure their own power under the new king.

A key group of faithful leaders refused to join Adonijah's rebellion. This group included Zadok the priest, Benaiah the commander of the royal bodyguard, Nathan the prophet, and David's elite warriors. They stayed completely loyal to King David and waited on God's choice for the next ruler.

Adonijah held a large sacrificial feast at the stone of Zoheleth near the spring of En-rogel, just south of Jerusalem. He invited all his royal brothers and the royal officials from the tribe of Judah to win their support. Offering sacrifices made his bid for the crown look like it had God's blessing.

Adonijah intentionally left out Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, David's bodyguard, and his younger brother Solomon. Leaving them off the guest list showed that he knew they supported Solomon and would never accept his revolt. It also made it clear that he viewed these men as dangerous rivals.

Nathan went quickly to Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon, to warn her about the secret takeover. He told her that Adonijah had already begun acting as king without David knowing anything about it. As God's prophet, Nathan knew he had to act fast to protect the Lord's plan for the throne.

Nathan urged Bathsheba to follow his advice so she could save both her life and Solomon's life. In the ancient world, a ruler who seized the throne through a revolt usually murdered rival heirs and their mothers to prevent future rebellions. Nathan knew they were in immediate mortal danger if Adonijah succeeded.

Nathan told Bathsheba to go straight to David and remind him of his solemn oath that Solomon would rule next. God had already revealed that Solomon was His chosen successor, and David had promised her this under oath. She was to ask the king plainly why Adonijah was taking over the throne instead.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars argue that David never actually made this oath, suggesting that Bathsheba and Nathan invented the promise to convince the failing king to choose Solomon.

notes.meaning: Nathan promised that while Bathsheba was still talking to the king, he would enter the room and back up her words. In the royal court, an urgent matter needed more than one credible witness to be taken seriously. Having the prophet confirm her story would move David to take immediate action.

Bathsheba followed Nathan's advice and entered the king's private bedroom. David was bedridden because of his old age and frail body, and Abishag was there attending to his needs. The scene highlights how weak and secluded the great king had become in his final days.

Bathsheba bowed low to the ground with deep reverence before the king. Even as David's wife, she approached him with the formal honor due to Israel's sovereign. David saw her humble posture and asked what urgent request she had brought.

Bathsheba reminded David of the solemn promise he had made before the Lord to place Solomon on the throne. She appealed to the king's faith and honor, knowing he took his vows before God very seriously. Her words put the duty of keeping faith with God directly before him.

Bathsheba explained that Adonijah had already taken the title of king while David was unaware of it. By gently adding that David did not know, she cleared the king of any wrongdoing while exposing his son's treason. Adonijah was moving behind his father's back to steal the royal authority.

Bathsheba told the king that Adonijah had sacrificed many animals and invited the army commander, the priest, and all the royal princes. She emphasized that Solomon alone had been excluded from the feast. This made it obvious that Adonijah did not view Solomon as an ally, but as a rival to be eliminated.

Bathsheba told David that the entire nation of Israel was waiting for him to name his successor. The people had not fully committed to Adonijah because they recognized that the decision belonged to the king alone. David still had the authority to settle the matter and declare who would sit on his throne.

Bathsheba warned David that as soon as he died, she and Solomon would be treated as dangerous traitors. When a ruler seized power without approval, any other claimants to the throne were usually killed. She appealed to David's love and justice to protect them before it was too late.

Just as Bathsheba finished speaking, Nathan the prophet arrived at the royal bedroom as planned. His prompt entrance matched their agreement to present a second witness to the king. The timing helped confirm Bathsheba's words and urged David to act without delay.

The attendants announced Nathan, and the prophet entered and bowed facedown before David. Even though the king was frail and in bed, Nathan gave him the full honor due to God's anointed leader. His deep reverence showed that he still regarded David as the true ruler of Israel.

Nathan asked David if he had secretly authorized Adonijah to rule after him. Nathan knew the king had not done this, but framing the question this way forced David to face the crisis directly. It made it clear that if David had not commanded this, Adonijah was in open rebellion.

Nathan reported that Adonijah had gone down to the valley, sacrificed many animals, and gathered the army officers and the priest. He told David that the crowd was already eating, drinking, and shouting, 'Long live King Adonijah!' The revolt was no longer hidden, but was being celebrated openly.

Nathan concluded by listing those who were deliberately excluded: himself, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the bodyguard commander, and Solomon. This selective snub revealed Adonijah's hostile intentions toward David's most loyal servants. It showed that the new faction was actively trying to overthrow the king's faithful inner circle.
